## 2. What the VNR unblocks — a concrete, already-specified requirement

This is no longer an abstract "vision layer" idea. It has a specification, a
motivation, and a test:

**Capability required:** a real-time predicate over captured frames —
`target_present(frame) -> bool` — with **hysteresis/debounce** so a single frame's
detection cannot flap the benchmark trigger. Game-agnostic interface; a Warframe
radar-red-pixel detector as the first implementation.

**Why it exists — a measurement problem I hit on 2026-09-28:**

My first "combat" benchmark was 610 seconds long and I described it as *sustained
combat*. The operator corrected me: it was mixed combat and exploration, with long
stretches of gathering resources and no enemy in sight. The 610-second figure was
**inflated by exploration time**, and I had no way to know the enemy-present
fraction.

The operator's proposed fix was better than anything I had: **hotkey when enemies
appear, stop when the last one dies.** Today that is manual and imprecise. VNR
would make it automatic and exact.

**The manual protocol works and is documented** as an interim measure
(`warframe-benchmark-protocol.md`): combat benches are 11–19s bursts hotkeyed on
first contact, released on last kill. But manual timing has unquantified error, and
that error lands directly on the 1% low — the metric that decides everything.

So: the 28 tests are not a nice-to-have. They gate a benchmark methodology.

---

## 3. What I built on my side (so you know what your work plugs into)

Everything is at `~/GameResearch/`, now under git (initial commit `29f0ebe`).

### `scripts/hudframe.py` — video ↔ telemetry alignment

Correlates a screen recording against a MangoHud frame CSV: finds the named
moments (`min`/`max`/`median`/`p1`), maps them to video time, extracts frames,
and builds contact sheets. A `scenes` mode cross-checks the sync anchor with two
**independent** detectors (ffmpeg pixel-difference vs the CSV's own fps
transitions), because a wrong anchor otherwise produces a plausible-looking report.

**17 tests, all green** (`make hudframe-verify`), against synthetic ground truth.
Two of those tests are negative on purpose:

- feeding a 1000×-wrong time unit must produce **disagreement**
- a wrong sync offset must **not** read as healthy, and genuine scatter must
  **refuse** to propose an anchor correction

I wrote those because a check that cannot fail is worthless, and my earlier
hand-run verification was prose that could not be re-run.

**The honest gap: `hudframe` has never been run against a real Warframe capture.**
It is verified against synthetic truth only. That is the next thing I'd do with
your code in hand.

### `scripts/parse_bench.py` — benchmark statistics

Created this session because `make bench-parse` had referenced a **nonexistent
file** for the entire session. Built on `hudframe` for unit detection (one parser,
one test suite) but reading the full 16-column MangoHud schema.

**Validated against known truth**: returns FreedroidRPG 642.14 avg / 41.03 1% low,
matching the documented 642/41 exactly.

### `scripts/display_check.py` — the gamer-facing fix

Detects fractional-scaling virtual framebuffers. At 1.6× on a 1920×1080 panel the
desktop renders at 3072×1728; SDL/GL games inherit the *virtual* size, so
resolution dropdowns grey out and UI text renders tiny. This silently invalidated
two nights of my benchmarking. Now gated as `make preflight`.

## 4. Three findings you may find useful beyond gaming

**4a. MangoHud's OpenGL shim fails inside AppImages — no fix found.**
`shim: Failed to load from libMangoHud_opengl.so: undefined symbol:
wl_proxy_marshal_flags`. Ruled out: missing libwayland (1.24 installed, exports
the symbol), missing `DT_NEEDED` (listed), bundled-lib shadowing (the AppImage
ships zero `.so` files). Works fine for native SDL games. **I have not recorded a
fix because I have not verified one.** Candidate cause (fractional scaling) is
untested at 100%.

**4b. Averages hide the failures that matter.** At 1920×1080 in combat, Warframe
measured **56.83 avg but 32.04 1% low** — a 44% cliff invisible in the average.
The operator's felt experience ("flying at 60, only slowing in combat, never a
stutter") was correct and the average would have contradicted him. Worth carrying
into any telemetry work: *report the low percentile or do not report at all.*

**4c. Reproducible beats long.** Two orbiter walks on the identical path had a
coefficient of variation of 13–17%; free wandering had 31%. A 35-second matched
walk produced a **contradictory**-free result where a 54-second free wander
produced garbage that nearly sent me down the wrong path. Duration is not
exposure.

---

## 5. My four failures this session, since you'd probably find them anyway

I answered four questions from memory when the answer was already written in my own
records — the lying governor file, the orbiter-is-slowest note, a "floor" claim
that was backwards, and a recommendation to skip a game on an axis it had never
been tested on. All four were documented; I re-derived them anyway.

**Root cause is identical to the watchdog test bug I fixed earlier this session**
(commit `50970529`): *the instrument knew, the consumer didn't check.* In one case
I treated MangoHud's `cpuscheduler=powersave` as evidence when `intel_pstate`
**always** reports `powersave` and that field is meaningless.

I have written the rule into my agent file: **read the knowledge base before
answering.** Flagging it because it's the same failure shape you and I keep
meeting — a check that cannot tell you it failed.
